title: Slices: Length, Capacity & append
summary: A **slice** is Go's flexible, growable view over an array. It's a small three-word header — a pointer to a backing array, a **length**, and a **capacity** — which is the key to understanding `append`, sharing, and the occasional surprising bug.

subtopics.title: The slice header (ptr, len, cap)
subtopics.explanation: A slice value is three words: a pointer to an element in a backing array, the length (how many elements you can index), and the capacity (how many fit before a reallocation). Copying a slice copies the header, not the data. This three-word header is the whole basis for understanding a slice's length, capacity, and how append behaves.

subtopics.title: length vs capacity
subtopics.explanation: len(s) is how many elements the slice currently holds; cap(s) is how many it can hold before append must allocate a bigger array. You can re-slice up to cap without copying. Length and capacity are two of the three header fields, and their gap is exactly the room append fills before it must grow.

subtopics.title: How append grows
subtopics.explanation: If there's spare capacity, append writes into the existing array and returns a slice with a larger len. If not, it allocates a new, larger array (often ~2x), copies the elements, and returns a slice pointing at the new array. Always assign the result: s = append(s, x). Watching len and cap change across appends is the clearest window into how a slice's capacity governs reallocation.

subtopics.title: Slicing aliases the same array
subtopics.explanation: s[1:3] shares the backing array with s, so writing through one can change the other — until an append forces a reallocation. This aliasing is a common source of bugs. It falls directly out of the slice header: a sub-slice is just a new header pointing into the same backing array.

subtopics.title: nil vs empty slice
subtopics.explanation: A nil slice (var s []int) has len 0, cap 0, and no backing array, but you can still append to it. It's idiomatic to return a nil slice for 'no results'. A nil slice is simply a zero-valued slice header, which is why append and range handle it gracefully.

subtopics.title: copy() for independent data
subtopics.explanation: The built-in copy(dst, src) copies min(len(dst), len(src)) elements between slices and returns that count. Because slicing only shares the backing array, copy is how you get an independent duplicate that a later write won't leak into the original. It is the deliberate antidote to the aliasing that the slice header otherwise creates.

foundations.overview: Arrays in Go have a fixed size baked into their type, which makes them rigid. Slices fix that: a slice is a lightweight, growable window onto an underlying array. Almost all 'list' code in Go uses slices, so understanding their three-word header — pointer, length, capacity — is essential to writing correct, efficient Go.
foundations.formalDefinition: A slice is a descriptor (pointer, length, capacity) referencing a contiguous section of a backing array, providing dynamically-sized, flexible access to its elements.
foundations.whyItMatters: Slices are everywhere in Go, and the way append and slicing interact with the backing array is one of the most-tested topics in Go interviews and a frequent real-world bug source.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a long shelf (the backing array) and a movable bracket marking a section of it: the start (pointer), how many books are in the bracket (length), and how much room remains to the end of the shelf (capacity).
commonUseCases: Returning nil slices for empty results

commonMisconceptions.myth: append always modifies the original slice.
commonMisconceptions.reality: If capacity is exceeded, append allocates a new array; the original is unchanged. That's why you must write s = append(s, x).
s[i:j] shares the same backing array — no copy. Use copy() or append to a fresh slice if you need an independent copy.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A nil slice can't be used.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You can append to and range over a nil slice; len and cap are 0.

checkpoints.code:
s := make([]int, 0, 3)
s = append(s, 1, 2)
fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
checkpoints.explanation: make([]int, 0, 3) gives len 0, cap 3. Appending two elements raises len to 2; capacity is unchanged at 3 because 2 fits within it.

options: append is not allowed in functions
The function gets a copy of the header; append may reallocate, leaving a's header unchanged
checkpoints.explanation: add receives a copy of the slice header. If append reallocates (or even if it doesn't grow a's len), the caller's header is never updated. To mutate the caller's slice, return the result: a = add(a).

checkpoints.prompt: Pre-allocate a slice that holds 0 elements now but won't reallocate until 100.
checkpoints.codeAfter: for i := 0; i < 100; i++ { buf = append(buf, i) }
checkpoints.explanation: make([]int, 0, 100) gives length 0 with capacity 100, so the 100 appends never reallocate. make([]int, 100) would start with 100 zero-valued elements instead.

codeLab.title: Deduplicate while preserving order
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Solve(nums []int) []int` that returns the elements of nums with duplicates removed, keeping first-seen order. Pre-size your result.
hints: Use a map[int]bool to remember which values you've already added.
Pre-size the output with make([]int, 0, len(nums)) to avoid growth copies.
Append only when the value hasn't been seen, which preserves first-seen order.

debuggingLab.title: append seems to do nothing
debuggingLab.symptom: After the loop, s is still empty.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: append returns a new slice header (possibly pointing at a new array). Discarding the return value throws away the grown slice, so s never changes. (In real Go this is also a compile error: 'append return value not used'.)
commonMistakes: Calling append without assigning its result.
Assuming append mutates the slice variable in place.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Assign the result of append back to s.

theory.question: What is the difference between a slice's length and capacity?
theory.directAnswer: Length is how many elements the slice currently contains (what you can index and range over); capacity is how many elements fit in the backing array starting from the slice's first element before append must allocate a new, larger array. len(s) <= cap(s) always.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two of the three fields in the slice header (the third is the pointer).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Capacity lets append grow without reallocating every time, amortizing the cost of growth.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: append fills unused capacity in place; when it runs out, it allocates a bigger array (often ~2x) and copies.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing the two leads to reallocation surprises and aliasing bugs — a classic interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: make([]byte, 0, 4096) pre-allocates a 4KB buffer so building a response appends without repeated reallocations.

followUps.question: How can you check capacity?
followUps.answer: With the built-in cap(s); len(s) gives the length.

followUps.question: What growth factor does append use?
followUps.answer: Implementation-defined — historically ~2x for small slices and ~1.25x for large ones; never rely on an exact number.

theory.question: Why must you write `s = append(s, x)` instead of just `append(s, x)`?
theory.directAnswer: Because append may return a slice with a different length and even a different backing-array pointer (if it had to reallocate). The original slice header is passed by value, so unless you assign the returned header back, your variable won't see the new length or array.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The assignment that captures append's returned (possibly relocated) slice header.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Slices are value headers; append can't mutate the caller's variable, only return a new header.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: If capacity suffices, the returned header points at the same array with a larger len; otherwise it points at a new array.

theory.whyImportant: Forgetting the assignment is one of the most common Go beginner bugs.
theory.realWorldExample: Building a slice in a loop silently stays empty if you forget to assign append's result.

followUps.question: What happens to other slices that aliased the old array after a reallocation?
followUps.answer: They keep pointing at the old array, so they no longer see elements appended to the reallocated slice.

theory.question: What is a nil slice, and how does it behave compared to an empty slice?
theory.directAnswer: A nil slice is the zero value of a slice type (var s []int): its pointer is nil and its length and capacity are both 0, with no backing array. It is safe to range over and to append to, and comparing it with nil returns true. An empty-but-non-nil slice (e.g. []int{} or make([]int, 0)) also has length 0 but is not equal to nil. For most operations — len, range, append — the two behave identically.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A slice header with a nil pointer and zero length and capacity.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So that a declared-but-uninitialized slice is immediately usable without a special constructor.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: append to a nil slice allocates a fresh backing array on the first element; len and range treat it as having zero elements.

theory.whyImportant: Returning a nil slice for 'no results' is idiomatic, and knowing nil is usable prevents unnecessary make() calls and nil checks.
theory.realWorldExample: A query function returns a nil slice when there are no matching rows; callers can range over it directly without guarding for nil.

followUps.question: When does the nil-vs-empty distinction actually matter?
followUps.answer: Mainly in equality checks (s == nil) and in JSON encoding, where a nil slice marshals to null but an empty slice marshals to [].

theory.question: What does the built-in copy(dst, src) do, and why would you use it instead of slicing?
theory.directAnswer: copy(dst, src) copies min(len(dst), len(src)) elements from src into dst and returns the number of elements copied. Unlike slicing, which produces another header sharing the same backing array, copy moves data into a separate array you already own — so later writes to one slice do not leak into the other.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A built-in that duplicates elements between two slices element-by-element.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Slicing never copies data, so a deliberate mechanism is needed to obtain an independent duplicate.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: It writes up to the shorter of the two lengths; you typically make a destination sized to len(src) first, then copy into it.

theory.whyImportant: copy is the standard antidote to slice aliasing bugs and the safe way to hand out data you keep mutating internally.
theory.realWorldExample: A parser that reuses one read buffer copies each token into a fresh slice before returning it, so the next read does not overwrite prior results.

followUps.question: What happens if dst is shorter than src?
followUps.answer: Only len(dst) elements are copied and the rest of src is ignored; copy returns len(dst).

followUps.question: Can copy work between overlapping slices of the same array?
followUps.answer: Yes — copy handles overlapping source and destination correctly, like memmove.

scenario.question: Two parts of your code share a slice; after one appends to it, the other occasionally sees corrupted/extra data. What's going on?
scenario.directAnswer: They share the same backing array. Appending within remaining capacity writes into that shared array, so the other view can see the change; once an append reallocates, the two diverge unpredictably. Give each owner an independent copy (copy() into a fresh slice) or use full-slice expressions s[low:high:max] to cap capacity and force copies.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Aliasing through a shared backing array.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Slicing never copies data — it creates another header over the same array.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: append into spare capacity mutates shared memory; a reallocation silently breaks the alias.

scenario.whyImportant: Shared-slice aliasing is a notorious real-world bug class.
scenario.realWorldExample: Returning sub-slices of a reused parsing buffer leaks later overwrites into earlier results.

followUps.question: What does the three-index slice s[a:b:c] do?
followUps.answer: It sets capacity to c-a, so a later append on the sub-slice can't write past c into the shared array — it reallocates instead.

scenario.question: A profiler shows your request handler spends most of its time in slice growth allocations while building a large result set. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: You are appending into a slice that started with zero capacity, so append repeatedly allocates a bigger backing array and copies the existing elements each time it overflows. If you know (or can estimate) the final size, pre-size the slice with make([]T, 0, n) so the appends fill spare capacity without reallocating and copying.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Repeated reallocation-and-copy caused by growing a slice from empty.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: append amortizes growth by allocating a larger array (often ~2x) when capacity runs out, but each growth still copies all existing elements.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Pre-allocating capacity up front means every append fits within cap, so no growth copy ever runs during the loop.

scenario.whyImportant: Uncontrolled slice growth in hot paths is a common, easily-fixed source of CPU and allocation pressure in Go services.
scenario.realWorldExample: Collecting N database rows into a slice: make([]Row, 0, expectedRows) turns dozens of growth copies into a single allocation.

followUps.question: What if you don't know the exact size in advance?
followUps.answer: Use a reasonable estimate for capacity; even an approximate pre-size cuts most reallocations, and append still grows safely if you exceed it.

systemDesign.question: You are designing a reusable byte buffer that gets refilled and processed thousands of times per second. How do slice length and capacity guide the design?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Allocate the backing array once with make([]byte, 0, size) so capacity stays fixed, then reset the buffer between uses by re-slicing to length zero (buf = buf[:0]) rather than allocating a new slice. This keeps the same backing array — capacity is preserved — so subsequent appends reuse the existing memory and avoid per-cycle allocations, which is critical for throughput and GC pressure.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A pooled, reusable buffer built on the slice header's separation of length and capacity.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: High-frequency processing cannot afford a fresh allocation and GC churn on every cycle.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: buf[:0] sets length to 0 while keeping the pointer and capacity, so append refills the same array; only if a cycle exceeds capacity does a reallocation occur.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Reusing capacity via buf[:0] is a foundational Go performance pattern used in the standard library (e.g. bytes.Buffer, sync.Pool consumers).
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A log-line encoder resets its scratch buffer with buf = buf[:0] before formatting each record, reusing one allocation across millions of lines.

followUps.question: Why not use make([]byte, 0) each cycle instead?
followUps.answer: That discards the previous backing array, forcing a new allocation and eventual GC work every cycle; re-slicing to buf[:0] keeps the capacity you already paid for.

followUps.question: What risk comes with reusing a buffer that you hand out to callers?
followUps.answer: Aliasing — if a caller retains a sub-slice, the next refill overwrites their data, so you must copy() out anything a caller keeps.

coding.question: Implement `func Reverse(s []int)` that reverses a slice in place.
coding.thoughtProcess: Swap the two ends moving inward with a two-pointer loop. Because a slice header shares the backing array, mutating elements in the function is visible to the caller — no return needed.
coding.lineByLine: Two indices start at the ends and move toward the middle; the parallel assignment swaps them without a temp. The loop stops when they meet. Since the slice shares its backing array with the caller, the caller sees the reversal.

followUps.question: Why doesn't Reverse need to return the slice?
followUps.answer: It mutates the shared backing array in place; the caller's slice sees the same elements.

followUps.question: Would this work for a string?
followUps.answer: Not directly — strings are immutable; you'd convert to []rune (or []byte for ASCII), reverse, then convert back.

coding.question: Implement `func RemoveAt(s []int, i int) []int` that removes the element at index i while preserving order, and returns the resulting slice.
coding.thoughtProcess: To delete an element without leaving a hole, shift the tail left over the removed slot. The idiomatic way is append(s[:i], s[i+1:]...), which copies the elements after i onto the elements starting at i and returns a slice one shorter. This reuses the same backing array, so it is O(1) space.
coding.lineByLine: First we bounds-check i and return the slice unchanged if it is out of range. Otherwise s[:i] is everything before the removed element, and s[i+1:]... spreads everything after it; append copies that tail down over index i and returns a slice with length reduced by one. Because it writes into the existing backing array, no new allocation is needed.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) — the tail after i is copied one position left.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — the removal reuses the original backing array.

followUps.question: Does the caller's original slice still see the old data?
followUps.answer: The backing array is mutated in place, so the caller must use the returned (shorter) slice; the old element at the last position is now stale.

followUps.question: How would you delete without preserving order, faster?
followUps.answer: Swap the last element into index i and re-slice: s[i] = s[len(s)-1]; return s[:len(s)-1] — O(1), but it reorders the slice.

keyTakeaways: A slice is a three-word header: pointer to a backing array, length, and capacity.
append fills spare capacity in place, then reallocates a larger array and copies — always write s = append(s, x).
Slicing (s[i:j]) shares the backing array; use copy() or a fresh slice to get independent data.
Pre-size with make([]T, 0, n) in hot paths to avoid repeated growth allocations, and watch for aliasing bugs.
